Depression and Addiction: What Do They Look Like?

Depression and addiction are two of the most common psychological problems that affect people’s everyday lives. To diagnose them consistently, doctors and psychologists use the ICD — the International Classification of Diseases. This shared system means that whichever doctor a patient sees, the same pattern of symptoms should lead to the same diagnosis, rather than diagnosis depending on one doctor’s personal judgement.

Key Fact

The ICD gives doctors a shared list of symptoms and features for each condition. A diagnosis is made by matching a patient’s symptoms against this list, not by personal opinion.

Symptoms of Depression

According to the ICD, depression is marked by a persistent low mood and a loss of interest or pleasure in activities a person once enjoyed. For a diagnosis, several symptoms must occur together for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks.

  • Persistent low mood, sadness or feelings of hopelessness
  • Loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyable activities
  • Low energy and fatigue, even after resting
  • Poor concentration, disturbed sleep or appetite, and feelings of worthlessness or guilt

Doctors do not diagnose depression from a single symptom appearing once. The ICD requires several of these features to appear together and to last for a sustained period. This is what separates ordinary sadness, which everyone experiences from time to time, from clinical depression that affects a person’s ability to function.

Symptoms of Addiction

Addiction is identified by a cluster of features rather than one behaviour on its own. The ICD lists several signs that, together, point to addiction.

  • A strong compulsion or craving to use the substance or repeat the behaviour
  • Difficulty controlling how much is used or when it happens — loss of control
  • Tolerance, needing more of the substance to get the same effect
  • Withdrawal symptoms when use is reduced or stopped
  • Continuing use despite clear harm, and neglecting other interests or responsibilities

As with depression, a diagnosis of addiction depends on several of these features occurring together over time, not a single isolated incident. A person who occasionally drinks more than planned is not automatically diagnosed with addiction — the ICD looks for a repeated, compulsive pattern.

Key Fact

Depression is defined by persistent low mood and loss of interest lasting at least two weeks. Addiction is defined by compulsion, loss of control, tolerance, withdrawal and continued use despite harm.

How Has Incidence Changed Over Time?

Reported rates of depression and addiction have risen over recent decades. This does not necessarily mean far more people are affected than in the past — part of the change reflects how mental health problems are noticed, discussed and recorded. Three factors help explain the trend.

Increased challenges of modern living. Greater isolation, financial pressure and work demands are widely seen as more common than in previous generations. Reduced face-to-face contact and constant connectivity through technology can increase loneliness, a known risk factor for both depression and addictive behaviour.

Increased recognition of symptoms. Depression and addiction are now better understood by clinicians and the public. As awareness grows, people are more likely to recognise their own experiences as symptoms of a genuine problem and seek help, which raises recorded figures even where the true number of cases has changed less dramatically.

Lessening of social stigma. Admitting to depression or addiction once risked shame, judgement or discrimination. As public attitudes have shifted, through campaigns and more open discussion, more people feel able to disclose their difficulties and access treatment, which further increases reported incidence.

Effects on Individuals

Depression and addiction affect every part of a person’s life. They can cause damage to relationships, since withdrawal, irritability, secrecy or changed behaviour make it difficult to maintain friendships, romantic partnerships and family bonds. They create difficulties coping with day-to-day life, such as getting to work, managing money or keeping up with basic self-care. Both conditions are also linked to a negative impact on physical wellbeing — disrupted sleep, poor nutrition, reduced activity and, in the case of addiction, direct physical harm from repeated use of the substance itself.

Effects on Society

Depression and addiction also place pressure on wider society. There is an increased need for social care, as more people require support from health and social services that are already stretched. Addiction in particular has been linked to increased crime rates, since some individuals may commit offences to fund a habit or behave differently while under the influence. There are also serious implications for the economy: lost productivity and absenteeism from work linked to depression and addiction together cost billions of pounds each year in lost output and treatment.

The spec treats depression and addiction as clinical, educational topics to be studied, not as labels for individuals. This lesson is designed to build understanding of these conditions as areas of psychological study, not to diagnose anyone. Describing symptoms and effects accurately, and without sensationalising them, is itself a valued exam skill — examiners reward precise, measured language over dramatic description.

Judging the Quality of Psychological Research

Two ideas run through every part of the Edexcel specification: reliability and validity. A reliable study gives the same results again and again. A valid study actually measures the thing it set out to measure. The two are not the same — a study can be reliable but not valid, for example if a test consistently measures something other than what the researcher intended.

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency of results on repeated occasions. Validity = accuracy — whether the study truly measures what it claims to and whether findings apply beyond the study itself. Edexcel requires you to judge the reliability and validity of sampling methods, experimental designs, and quantitative and qualitative data.

Reliability and Validity of Sampling Methods

The way a sample is chosen affects how far results can be trusted beyond the people actually tested — this is generalisability. Random and stratified sampling tend to produce samples that better represent the target population, improving generalisability. Volunteer and opportunity sampling are quicker but risk a biased sample — for example, volunteers may be more motivated or confident than the average person, reducing how far the findings can be generalised.

Reliability and Validity of Experimental Designs

Repeated measures designs use the same participants in every condition, removing participant variables as an explanation for any difference found — this can improve validity. However, taking part in more than one condition risks order effects, which can reduce reliability unless controlled. Independent measures designs avoid order effects, which supports reliability, but participant variables between the separate groups can threaten validity if the groups differ in an important way before the study even begins.

Reliability and Validity of Quantitative and Qualitative Methods

Quantitative data (numbers, such as reaction times or test scores) is usually easier to check for reliability, because the same measurement can be repeated and compared directly. However, numbers alone can miss the depth of an experience, which can limit validity. Qualitative data (words, such as interview transcripts) can capture rich detail about how someone actually thinks or feels, supporting validity, but it is harder to check for reliability because different researchers may interpret the same words differently.

Edexcel expects you to weigh up studies using six issues: validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics, objectivity, and subjectivity. A structured laboratory experiment tends to score well on reliability and objectivity because procedures are standardised and measurements are numerical. A case study or unstructured interview may score well on validity, because it captures depth and detail, but poorly on reliability and objectivity, because the researcher’s own interpretation shapes the data.

Ethical Issues in Psychological Research

Because psychological research studies real people, researchers must deal responsibly with five named ethical issues: informed consent, deception, confidentiality, the right to withdraw, and protection of participants. Understanding each issue means knowing what it is and knowing a practical way a researcher deals with it.

Informed consent means participants are told what the study involves before they agree to take part. Researchers deal with this by giving a written information sheet and asking participants to sign a consent form. Where participants are children, as in Piaget and Inhelder’s Three Mountains task, a parent or guardian gives consent on the child’s behalf.

Deception happens when participants are not told the true aim of a study, or are misled about it. Researchers only use deception when it is unavoidable — for example, when knowing the aim would change how people behave — and they deal with it by fully explaining the true purpose in a debrief afterwards.

Confidentiality means personal data is kept private. Researchers deal with this by storing data anonymously, using numbers or initials instead of names, and only reporting results in a way that does not identify any individual.

The right to withdraw means a participant can leave the study at any time, and can ask for their data to be removed even after taking part. Researchers deal with this by reminding participants of this right at the start and during debriefing, and by never pressuring anyone to continue.

Protection of participants means researchers must not expose people to risks greater than everyday life. Researchers deal with this by stopping a study if a participant becomes distressed, and by offering support after any study that could cause upset.

Key Fact

The five named ethical issues are: informed consent (information sheet and signed agreement), deception (only when unavoidable, resolved by a full debrief), confidentiality (anonymous data storage), right to withdraw (can leave, or remove data, at any time without penalty), and protection of participants (no more risk than everyday life; support offered if needed).

Ethical issues appear throughout the compulsory topics. Piaget and Inhelder’s Three Mountains task and Gunderson et al.’s praise study both involved children, so parental informed consent and protection from distress were essential. Caspi et al.’s study of genes and depression involved sensitive personal and medical information, raising confidentiality concerns about how genetic data was stored and reported. Young’s study of CBT for internet addiction involved real clients in treatment, raising confidentiality of therapy records and protection from harm during sensitive discussions.

Haney, Banks and Zimbardo’s simulated prison study is a well-known case where protection of participants broke down: some ‘prisoners’ experienced real psychological distress, and the study was stopped early. It raises questions about whether the right to withdraw was genuinely respected when participants felt they were playing an assigned role. Piliavin et al.’s subway field study used deception — passengers did not know they were part of an experiment and could not give informed consent in advance — which is typical of field experiments and raises the question of whether a debrief was practical at all.

Ethical Issues as an Ongoing Debate

An ethical issue is any concern about how a study’s design or conduct might affect participants’ rights or wellbeing. Psychology is often described as facing a trade-off: valuable scientific knowledge sometimes requires methods, like deception or distressing scenarios, that create ethical risk. This debate runs across all five compulsory topics — from studying children’s cognitive development to studying obedience and conformity — and examiners expect you to use content from more than one topic to discuss it.

Key Fact

Ethical issues are not abstract rules — they show up in real named studies across every compulsory topic. Being able to name the issue, explain why it arose in a specific study, and state the practical way of dealing with it is what earns marks in Edexcel’s extended questions.

Working with Data

Collecting data is only the first step in psychological research. Once a study has been run, the researcher must organise, summarise and display the results so that patterns become visible and conclusions can be drawn. This lesson covers the data-handling and descriptive-statistics skills you need for your exam — including the calculations you are expected to show working for.

Types of Data

Quantitative data is expressed as numbers, allowing direct comparison and calculation — for example, the number of words recalled in a memory test or a score on a rating scale. Qualitative data is expressed in words or descriptions, capturing meaning and detail that numbers cannot — for example, a participant’s account of what they were thinking during a task.

Primary data is collected directly by the researcher for their own study, such as running an experiment or conducting an interview. Secondary data was collected previously by someone else — published statistics or an earlier study, for example — and is re-analysed by the current researcher. It saves time but may not match the current research question exactly.

Key Fact

Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is in words. Primary data is collected first-hand by this researcher; secondary data was collected previously by someone else. Any dataset can combine these — for example, quantitative secondary data such as national exam results.

Mean, Median and Mode

The mean is found by adding all the values and dividing by how many there are. If five participants recalled 7, 8, 6, 9 and 5 words, the mean is $$\frac{7+8+6+9+5}{5} = \frac{35}{5} = 7$$ words. The mean uses every value, so it is sensitive to outliers — one very high or low score can pull it away from the typical value.

The median is the middle value once the data is ordered. With an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle numbers. Because it ignores extreme scores, the median is a better measure of the ‘typical’ result when outliers are present.

The mode is the value that appears most often. It is the only measure of central tendency that works with categorical data, such as the most common favourite colour in a sample, but it gives little information if scores are spread evenly.

Range

The range shows how spread out a dataset is: highest value minus lowest value. For the scores 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, the range is \(9 - 5 = 4\). A large range means participants performed very differently from each other; a small range means performance was consistent. Like the mean, the range is distorted by a single outlier.

Key Fact

Mean = total of all values divided by how many values there are. Median = middle value once ordered. Mode = most frequent value. Range = highest minus lowest. Mean and range are pulled about by outliers; the median is not.

Ratios, Fractions and Percentages

Edexcel expects you to convert and interpret data using ratios, fractions and percentages — skills tested directly in your exam. If a sample of 30 participants contains 18 women and 12 men, the ratio of women to men is \(18:12\), which simplifies to \(3:2\).

The same data can be expressed as a fraction: \(\frac{18}{30}\) of the sample were women, which simplifies to \(\frac{3}{5}\). Always simplify fractions to their lowest terms where possible — this shows the examiner you understand the relationship between the numbers, not just the raw values.

To convert a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100. \(\frac{18}{30} \times 100 = 60\%\) of the sample were women. Percentages let you compare groups of different sizes fairly — for instance, comparing the proportion of participants who conformed in two studies with different sample sizes.

Key Fact

Ratios compare two quantities with a colon (e.g. \(3:2\)). Fractions show a part out of a whole and should be simplified. Percentages are found by multiplying a fraction by 100 and let you compare proportions across different sample sizes.

Standard Form and Significant Figures

Psychological data can involve very large or very small numbers — for example, the number of neurons in the brain. Standard form writes these more manageably as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. For example, 86,000,000,000 neurons can be written as \(8.6 \times 10^{10}\).

You are also expected to round answers to an appropriate number of significant figures. A mean of 7.428571 words recalled should usually be rounded to a sensible level of precision, such as 7.4 (2 significant figures), rather than reported with excessive decimal places that imply false accuracy.

Displaying Quantitative Data

Frequency tables record how many times each value, or range of values, occurs. A bar chart displays separate categories as bars with gaps between them, showing the data is discrete. A histogram is used for continuous data, such as reaction times grouped into ranges, and has no gaps between bars because the underlying scale runs continuously.

A scatter diagram plots two variables against each other, with each point representing one participant’s pair of scores. If the points form a rough upward line, the variables show a positive correlation; a downward line shows a negative correlation; a random scatter with no pattern shows no correlation. Scatter diagrams let you translate numerical results into a visual pattern and are the standard way to display correlational data.

The Normal Distribution

Many psychological variables, when measured across a large population, form a normal distribution. This produces a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve when plotted: the mean, median and mode all fall at the same central point, and scores become progressively rarer as you move towards either tail.

Intelligence test scores are a classic example — most people score close to the average, with far fewer people scoring extremely high or extremely low. Psychologists use the normal distribution as a benchmark for judging how typical or unusual an individual score is, and many statistical tests assume the underlying data is approximately normally distributed.
